I was like this [gestures] waiting for my whipping. He grabbed me here [gesture] and he said, “Boy, don’t grow up being like they are. They are not going to be worth anything,” Daddy said. Then he went in. He said wasdi to Mom, “If these boys ever grow up,” - toward the north, Dad lived in Wisconsin for a while - “if they go there, they might, but I don’t think so,” he said. “But that one sitting there is probably going somewhere.” Which was me. He said, “If he goes there. There really is a lot of work there.” By God, if I didn’t end up in Wisconsin. Day one, when I got to Wisconsin, I went to work there. That’s where I stayed hooked up. phrases.english_text: Tommy Sanders came one time, when we were working at City Lake. My wife said, “Some old man came to visit you in a blue pickup. He needs to talk to you. It’s important.” So I waited. He said he will be back. And it was him, Tommy Sanders, and I haven’t seen him... the last time I seen him was at the Cherokee Children Mission. He said, “They said there is someone living here that is a Pettit.” He said, “I was wanting you to cut me a rick of wood if you have time.” So, I went with him to the Waterdown's. They had land right there by the Cherokee Children Mission School. We went in there, and I cut it for him. I didn’t split because he just wanted some for overnight. So I cut him a rick. So we were just sitting there, and he was carrying two of those old-timey lunch boxes. He had made bologna, coffee, and chips. We ate after I cut the wood for him. He said, “Billy,”- no, first he said, “Which one are you?” I said, “Billy.” He said, “That’s what I thought.” He said, “Do your boy’s children that you have go to school at Greasy?” He lives near there, by Greasy School.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, me too. I'm right there. If I help someone, like you said, they will want to pay. I will say, “Help the next person, because someone is going to need help.” Because I have had a lot of help in my lifetime and I just want to give some back, yep. There was an incident one time in Baldwin Wisconsin, when I was still living in Wisconsin. Me and a co-worker were driving, he was a machine operator. He had his seat pulled back. It was about 4:30 in the morning in Baldwin, going towards St. Croix Falls. No houses till like 12 or 15 miles, now there are houses everywhere. We were driving through nothing but cornfields. The corn was this high [gesture]. Out of the east came a car, and it sped up. Out of the west came another. I seen it. We were a way yet. I seen the signal light. It was going to turn where we were coming. Boy, it was coming from the east fast. He sped up his car. I said, “Gaw dernit, Rick! They are going to hit!” Rick heard me and said, “Who’s going to hit?” Soon as he did that, it was early in the morning, dark, no yard lights. All we had was lights on the cars. It just got dark. When they hit, it just turned all the lights out. A girl got killed that morning, so I parked the car on the side of the road and turned on the emergency lights. We ran over there. I went to help the one on this side, the one that got hit, and Rick went to help the one that done it. That girl, you could see that’s how she was laying down. When they hit, she went like this [gesture]. You could see her face that big on the windshield. She hit her head and broke her back. She was killed right there, and the other he was helping was like this [gesture] under the steering wheel. The gear shift was stuck right here. Not through the skull just through the skin it came out here [gesture]. I was trying to open the door so I could help them, but nothing. So I went around. It was pushed against the guard rail, and I could not get in over there. So, I ran back around this way and took my shirt off and wrapped it – I was going to break the window behind them. When I did this, someone said try this door. I had already tried that door. I was going to break the window out. I said, “I done did.” I thought Rick was standing there, and there was nobody else except me, Rick, and them people. So I said, “I done did.” He said, “Try again.” He had been hit right there [gesture]. He was just smashed. The man was in there, moaning. He said, “Tell him you are going to be with him in a minute.” I said, “Hold on, sir, I’m trying to get in to you. Just hold on,” I told him. I grabbed the door, and I done tried this door. The door opened like it was new. And this is God’s honest truth. He knows what I seen. He said, “Get in. He is badly hurt.” He told me to just lean over the seat, but he was talking in English. So I did what he said and followed it. When I grabbed that man, immediately all of my arm turned bloody. I told him what I was going to do. He said, “No, when you bring him back to the seat,” he said, “hold his head. He is really injured. Keep talking to him. Help is already coming.” Who called them? There was nobody. Cars didn’t even go by. So I stayed like that in the back. The blood was going like this here on my hands [gesture], talking to him. I did what the guy asked me to do. I did all of that. Then I seen state patrols. Two of them came. Before that, I seen what the man looked like. He didn’t have a face, and the car was hiding everything of him, but he did not have a face. I seen him. I told him OK. He was wearing red, a red and black shirt. I even put it in the state patrol statement as a witness. I wrote it all down, what I seen. So I told the state patrol. “How long ago did you do this training?” he said. I told him I ain't never done nothing like this. “How did you know what to do?” he said. I said, “That guy out there.” I grabbed him and said, “That guy out there told me what to do.” He said, “What guy?” I said, “There is a guy.” I told him what he had on. They both shined their spotlights and looked around. Nobody was anywhere around. So I said, “Rick, where did that guy go?” I said to him. He said, “What guy, Billy?” I said, “That guy that was just here.” He said, “There ain't no guy, Billy. It’s just us.” By God, he did not have a face. That is what that man told me. Out there, what I did for that man, I talked to him, I told him I wasn’t leaving him. The ambulance came. I was holding him all that time. He said, “Don’t let him go, this man, don’t let him go.” I crawled over the seat and held this man. I crawled over the seat with the ambulance people and they did that to him here. About eight months later, I was sitting at Fall Creek. I had just got back from work. My little girl – the phone rang, and I said, “Don’t answer it.” I was hungry. She quickly answered it. She said, “Hold on. Dad, it’s for you.” Man, I almost cussed. I got to the phone and said hello. They said, “Hello, is this Billy Pettit?” I said, “It’s Billy Pettit.” This is what happened: they said, “About eight months back, I was in a car accident.” Gah-lee, that’s what they said. I was back in that place. I quickly seen that man again. Y’know, there’s a smart—smartass talk… Y’know, he said, “You saved my life.” I almost said, “Did I kill a poop-eating dog?” I almost told him that, but I held my tongue. I said, “Oh, did I? How did I do this?” He said, “I was in a bad car accident. My neck was broke in three places. One bad move and I would have died underneath that steering wheel. You saved my life,” he said. Then I told him what all took place. He said, “Well, I want you to...” He told me his address. He said, “You are our family.” I didn’t even know the man. He said, “I want you to come and bring your family,” he said. “Let’s be as one.” That’s what happened – his neck was broke in three places. What that man said, he already knew how bad he was injured, and today he is still alive and well. Yeah, that’s what I am amazed with. Or I am not amazed. He didn’t have a face. I could not see his face. It was blank, but I seen everything else: his hair was brown, about this long [gesture]. I could see that because I wasn’t parked that far from it. They never found anyone. You can read my statement. I wrote everything I seen that morning.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, and long time ago when I was little, I guess I was sick all the time. I remember Mom would put blankets on me when it was hot, trying to sweat it out, I guess. One time I was laying there, Watie was laying on this side. Dad had already passed. I was laying in the middle and Mom on this side. I was laying there with a fever. Someone shined a light in our bedroom. They shined a light. I was laying there, and usually I’ll pull the covers up, afraid of the tsigilis. I was like this, laying there. They shined the light. And I looked at the light. It wasn’t even on, the light, it was so bright in there, the light bulb looked black. It looked burnt. Then I did this [gesture] and thought, “Where is it coming from?” I thought someone was up in the living room. But our bedroom was all lit up. I did this: I got up. It was standing there white against that door. He had his hands like this [gesture], standing there, and I know what I seen. When I tell people, they say you were probably next to death. Near-death experience, they say. No, it wasn’t. I was healed quickly. That was the last time I was sick. So I looked at it. It did not have a face. Again, I seen everything. I didn’t see no nail-scarred hands. He had them like this [gesture]. So I just laid back down. I was doing Mom like this, saying, “Mom” and that light slowly went off. Mom sat up, doing this [gesture], cleaning the tobacco from her mouth. She said, “What, little one?” OK, before I woke up, she was putting blankets on where I was laying or whatever I did. When I woke up, Mom was pressing here on my chest. She was talking to someone, and I didn’t know nothing about JESUS. She was talking to someone in the dark. She had it like this. I said, “Mom?” I went like this to her [gesture] and said, “Mom, what are you doing?” But she didn’t talk to me. So when she was done, she told him thank you, whoever it was. I was looking around to see who she was talking to. I thought I was hallucinating. There was nobody. She said, “When you get up in the morning, little one, you are not going to get sick anymore.” That is the last time I have been sick. Yeah, and I was like seven. I told Mom what I seen. She said, “Go to sleep.” So I went back to sleep. I woke up early in the morning and the chickens were crowing. Then I woke up Mom. I said, “Mom, Mom.” She said, “What is it, little one?” She grabbed me and started touching me. She said, “Gaw! You got healed!” I haven’t been sick since and that’s like 50-something years ago. I get a cold, but a fever, never.
